articles.title: USP30 Beyond Mitophagy: A Context-Dependent Deubiquitinase in Cancer Progression.
articles.abstract: Ubiquitin-specific protease 30 (USP30) is a mitochondrial outer membrane-associated deubiquitinase best known for antagonizing PTEN-induced kinase 1 (PINK1)/Parkin-dependent ubiquitination and suppressing mitophagy. This established role has linked USP30 to mitochondrial quality control and neurodegenerative diseases. However, emerging studies in cancer have expanded the biological scope of USP30, revealing functions that cannot be explained by mitophagy regulation alone. USP30 regulates diverse cancer-associated substrates through deubiquitination, thereby affecting protein abundance, subcellular localization, protein interactions, and downstream transcriptional programs. These substrate-dependent effects influence mitochondrial dynamics, lipid synthesis, glucose and amino acid metabolism, redox homeostasis, apoptosis, ferroptosis, epithelial-mesenchymal transition, cancer stemness, T-cell exhaustion, and therapy resistance. Although most studies indicate tumor-promoting roles of USP30 in hepatocellular carcinoma, breast cancer, colorectal cancer, oral squamous cell carcinoma, ovarian cancer, bladder cancer, prostate cancer, and leukemia models, context-dependent tumor-restraining activities have also been reported. In this Review, we examine cancer-associated functions of USP30 that extend beyond its established role in PINK1/Parkin-dependent mitophagy, discuss the spatial and substrate-dependent mechanisms underlying these activities, and highlight opportunities and challenges for therapeutic targeting.

articles.title: Spatially Segregated Electrochemical Sensor for Simultaneous Detection of Prostate-Specific Antigen and Sarcosine with Boosted Clinical Prediction of Early Prostate Cancer.
articles.abstract: Accurate early screening for prostate cancer (PCa) is critical to clinical decision-making. Simultaneous detection of the independent biomarkers sarcosine (Sar) and prostate-specific antigen (PSA) can improve screening accuracy for PCa through cross-validation. However, co-immobilizing the two detection units on the sensor surface causes close intermingling, leading to mutual interference between PSA and Sar detection, which severely reduces detection sensitivity. To address this issue, we adopted a spatial segregation strategy that allows Sar and PSA to be detected inside the pores and on the external surface of the metal-organic framework (MOF) sensors, respectively. First of all, we screened various MOFs through density functional theory calculations and adsorption experiments and found that MOF-74(Ni) outperformed other MOFs in adsorbing Sar. The nanozyme riboflavin (Rf) encapsulated within MOF-74 pores enables intracavity detection of small Sar molecules by size-sieving and cascade reaction. Concurrently, the ferrocene-labeled peptides (Pep-Fc), which are specifically cleavable by PSA, were immobilized on the surface to detect the large PSA molecules excluded from the pores. Finally, the MOF-74/Rf@Pep-Fc electrochemical sensor was constructed for spatial segregation detection. A series of results from adsorption kinetics and anti-interference experiments confirmed that this design can effectively eliminate the mutual interference between Sar and PSA. The sensor demonstrates a limit of detection of 0.78 fg/mL for Sar and 0.065 fg/mL for PSA. Clinical validation in serum showed that the sensor achieved 100% PCa predictive accuracy for PSA > 20 ng/mL, and in the 4-20 ng/mL range, simultaneous detection raised accuracy from < 50% to > 85%, highlighting its clinical potential.

articles.title: A structure-based virtual screening-driven discovery pharmaceutics platform for cancer therapeutics development: FDA 505(b)(2) repurposing of netupitant as a BMX-targeted nanomedicine using quality-by-design lipid nanoparticles and model-informed PBPK translation.
articles.abstract: Bone marrow tyrosine kinase on chromosome X (BMX) is an emerging therapeutic target implicated in prostate cancer progression, metastatic disease, and resistance to current therapies; however, no selective BMX-targeted therapy has advanced to clinical development. Building upon our previously established AI-driven BMX discovery platform, this study presents an integrated Discovery Pharmaceutics strategy combining artificial intelligence-assisted drug repurposing, Quality-by-Design (QbD)-guided lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation, experimental validation, and physiologically based pharmacokinetic (PBPK) modeling to accelerate clinical translation through the FDA 505(b)(2) regulatory pathway. An structure-based virtual screening workflow comprising 2,115 FDA-approved small molecules identified netupitant as one of the highest-ranked candidates against the BMX catalytic domain, exhibiting a predicted binding affinity of -10.9 kcal/mol together with favorable selectivity over closely related Tec-family kinases. Netupitant demonstrated concentration-dependent inhibition of prostate cancer cell growth with IC<sub>50</sub> values of 15.97 μM in DU145 cells and 7.1 μM in PC3 cells. A Box-Behnken Design optimized Netupitant-loaded lipid nanoparticles (Netupitant-LNPs) with a particle size of 133.9 ± 3.2 nm, polydispersity index of 0.213 ± 0.005, zeta potential of + 30 ± 1.3 mV, and encapsulation efficiency of 97.3 ± 0.7%. Cryogenic transmission electron microscopy confirmed uniformly dispersed spherical nanoparticles with an average diameter of 130 ± 6 nm, consistent with dynamic light scattering measurements. The nanoformulation substantially enhanced therapeutic efficacy, reducing IC<sub>50</sub> values to 1.1 μM in DU145 cells and 0.5 μM in PC3 cells, representing approximately 15-fold and 14-fold improvements, respectively, over free netupitant. To facilitate clinical translation, experimentally determined formulation characteristics were incorporated into a mechanistic Simcyp® Version 25.2 middle-out physiologically based pharmacokinetic model. The exploratory PBPK model compared alternative intravenous dosing scenarios and identified 100 mg once weekly as a candidate regimen for further evaluation; these simulations do not establish a clinical dosing recommendation. Collectively, this work demonstrates that integrating AI-enabled drug repurposing, Discovery Pharmaceutics, nanomedicine engineering, and model-informed drug development provides an effective strategy for accelerating oncology drug development. Netupitant-LNPs emerge as a repurposed nanomedicine candidate with predicted BMX binding while establishing a broadly applicable translational framework for FDA-approved drug repurposing through the 505(b)(2) pathway.

articles.title: From β-Blasts to α-Bombs: Bone-Targeting Radiopharmaceutical Therapies.
articles.abstract: Bone metastases are a significant source of morbidity in advanced malignancy, particularly in prostate cancer, because osteoblastic metastases can cause pain, skeletal-related events, and quality-of-life impairment. Bone-targeting radionuclide drugs are also effective in the treatment of increased bone turnover and were first developed as β-emitters for palliation but have been developed in recent years as α-emitters with proven survival benefit. This review covers the biology, history, and mechanism of action of the approved bone-targeting radiopharmaceuticals (<sup>89</sup>Sr-chloride, <sup>153</sup>Sm-lexidronam, <sup>223</sup>Ra-dichloride). Special focus is placed on the only bone-targeting radiopharmaceutical currently approved in the United States-<sup>223</sup>Ra-dichloride-including patient selection, administration, radiation safety, and follow-up. <sup>223</sup>Ra, a calcium analog with a short α-particle path length, high linear energy transfer, and marrow-sparing properties, is valuable in the treatment of metastatic androgen pathway modulator-resistant prostate cancer (formerly metastatic castration-resistant prostate cancer) with bone-predominant disease and symptoms. The practical aspects of nuclear medicine are emphasized, such as imaging confirmation, laboratory value thresholds, written instructions, room preparation, contamination control, discharge instructions, and posttreatment monitoring. Bone-targeting radiopharmaceutical therapy has increasingly attractive options beyond palliation with new combination and sequencing treatment options involving prostate-specific membrane antigen-targeted therapy. The lessons learned from the shift from "β-blasts" to "α-bombs" provide a potential pathway to more effective current treatment and a new generation of targeted radiopharmaceutical therapy.
